concepts.query:
Content Discovery

Content discovery is a discovery practice that studies an existing content collection itself: inventorying and auditing what it holds, and working out what that content means, how it is structured and how well it serves its purpose.

Contextual Research

Contextual research is a discovery practice that studies the conditions surrounding a product or content collection rather than the content or its users: the business, organizational, technical and market circumstances in which it exists.

Competitive Review

Competitive review is a contextual research method that assesses competitors' products, sites or services against criteria that matter to the organization commissioning it, showing where that organization stands and what its audiences already expect.

Heuristic Analysis

Heuristic analysis is a discovery method in which an expert reviews an existing site or product against established usability and user experience heuristics, identifying where it follows or departs from them without testing it with users.

Process Mapping

Process mapping is a contextual research method that documents and diagrams the business processes surrounding a product or content collection, particularly handoffs between systems and people, to expose inefficiencies and unintended consequences in how work actually gets done.

Stakeholder Engagement

Stakeholder engagement is a project management practice of identifying the people and groups with an interest in a project, learning what they need from it and what they can contribute, and keeping them informed and involved in its decisions throughout, so that their knowledge shapes the work and their concerns are addressed before they become obstacles.

User Research

User research is a discovery practice that studies the people a product or content collection serves, learning their behaviors, needs and motivations directly from them through observation, conversation and task-based methods.

Contextual Inquiry

Contextual inquiry is a user research technique used to understand behavior by either observing users in their real world environments, or staging scenarios to mimic those environments. Contextual inquiry uses direct observation to help to counter the recall and reporting bias that asking users about behavior can entail.

Mental Models

Mental model development is a user research technique that describes users' frames for understanding a service, product, topic, or set of content. Mental models can be elicited by single research techniques (such as card sorting) or synthesized from mixed methods. Mental models may be captured as narratives (for example with personas), a set of findings, or a graphical model such as a flow diagram.

User Interviews

User interviews are a user research method of focused one-to-one or small-group conversations that elicit how people think about a subject, along with their preferences and their behavior as they recall it. Interviews may include interactive tasks.

Best Practices

Best practices are a design approach of building on methods and conventions proven across many projects and contexts, and judging work against them, rather than solving each problem from first principles.

Collaborative Design

Collaborative design is a design approach in which the people with a stake in a solution, including clients, subject experts, users and the teams who will build and maintain it, take part in designing it, so that decisions draw on their combined knowledge and earn their shared commitment.

Design Principles

The formulation of design principles is a design approach in which a team states the fundamental rules a design must follow, specific to its problem, organization and audience, and uses them to make, explain and evaluate decisions consistently throughout the work.

Systems Thinking

Systems thinking is a design approach that treats a product, content collection or organization as a system of interacting parts, people and processes, attending to how they influence one another over time, including the delayed and nonlinear effects that make outcomes hard to predict.

Semantic Web

The semantic web is an engineering practice of making the meaning of data explicit, describing things and their relationships with shared, formally defined vocabularies so that software can integrate and reason over data from many sources. It spans the open web of data and the semantic layers organizations build over their own systems.

"Semantic web" refers to the web of "machine readable information," as opposed to the web of "pages." Semantic web applications are often built on technologies that support the encoding and inference of "meaning," including RDF, RDFS, and OWL.

Knowledge Graphs

A knowledge graph is an engineering outcome in which the entities of a domain and the typed relationships between them are represented as connected data that software can query and reason over, inferring facts that were never stated directly and integrating information from many sources.

Linked Data

Linked data is an engineering outcome in which the things a site or service describes are also published as structured statements that software can interpret, using shared vocabularies such as schema.org and identifiers that link to other data. On the web it is most often embedded in pages as JSON-LD.

Information Architecture

Information Architecture is the structural design of shared information spaces. Information architecture methods focus on organizing, structuring, and labeling content in an effective and sustainable way in order to help users find information and complete tasks.

Navigation Design

Navigation design is a user experience design practice that shapes how people move through a site or product: the navigation model, and the menus, links and signposts that show people where they are, where they can go and how to get there.

Search

Search is an information architecture practice concerned with a site's search system itself: how its index is built, how queries are parsed and results ranked for relevance, and how the results page, filters, autocomplete and synonyms help people retrieve a known item or refine an exploratory query.

Applies to writing about designing, configuring or tuning search: indexing, relevance ranking, query handling, search results interfaces and search log analysis.

Taxonomy

Taxonomy is an information architecture practice concerned with controlled vocabularies: the named, usually hierarchical sets of concepts an organization uses to classify content consistently, so that it can be retrieved, filtered and related through them. It spans a vocabulary's whole life, from designing it, to putting it to work in systems, to keeping it effective over time.

Includes taxonomy development, governance and implementation: designing a vocabulary, keeping it effective once it is in use, and putting it to work in systems, including migration between platforms and integration with them.

User Experience Design

User experience design is a design practice that shapes the whole of a person's experience with an organization, its services and its products, using research to coordinate content, tools and interactions across that experience rather than designing any one of them in isolation.

Interaction Design

Interaction design is a user experience design practice that specifies how a product responds to what people do: the actions available to them, the feedback they receive and the states an interface moves through, designed so that responses are predictable and coherent.

Automation

Automation is an engineering practice of handing repeatable tasks to software, so that they run on a trigger or a schedule with little or no human intervention. In content work it covers rule-based and model-driven handling of tasks such as tagging, transforming, validating and publishing content, wherever volume or consistency makes manual work impractical.

Python

Python is a general-purpose programming language, most often run on servers and from the command line, and widely used for data analysis, natural language processing and machine learning. It is valued for code that is easy to read and write, a large ecosystem of libraries and a large, supportive community.

Javascript

JavaScript is a programming language and, alongside HTML and CSS, a core technology of the web. Browsers run it to make pages interactive, from light, progressively enhanced features to frameworks such as React that render entire sites as single-page applications, and it also runs on servers through runtimes such as Node.js.

Technology Integration

Technology integration is an engineering practice of fitting new tools and services into an organization's existing systems, content and workflows, connecting them so that they exchange data and work as part of one process rather than as separate products. It covers the interfaces, configuration and changes to working practice that adoption requires.

Includes integrating AI models and services into content and publishing workflows.

Evaluation

Evaluation is a design practice that assesses whether a proposed or existing solution achieves what it was designed to achieve, by testing it with people, inspecting it against criteria or measuring how it performs.

Performance Evaluation

Performance evaluation is an evaluation method that assesses how quickly and efficiently a website or application delivers its content and functionality, including over slow connections and on less capable devices, and whether it makes people download more than their experience requires.

Usability Testing

Usability testing is an evaluation method in which representative users attempt realistic tasks with a product, prototype or body of content while researchers observe where they succeed, struggle or fail, in order to find and fix problems in its design.

Includes design prototype testing.

Accessibility Evaluation

Accessibility evaluation is an evaluation method that assesses whether people with disabilities can use a website or application, including people who rely on assistive technologies such as screen readers and keyboard navigation, and people with conditions such as low vision or motion sensitivity.

Content Modeling

Content modeling is an information architecture practice that defines the types of content an organization manages, the attributes each type is made of and the relationships between types, so that content can be managed as structured data and delivered across channels and platforms.

Content Strategy

Content strategy is a design practice that plans for the creation, publication and governance of content to meet established goals: deciding what content an organization needs, for whom and in what form, and how it will be produced and sustained over time.

Prototyping

Prototyping is building partial, provisional versions of a product, interface, content model or system in order to learn from them before committing to full production. As a design approach, it treats making as a way of thinking, testing ideas by building something people can try, react to and critique. As an engineering practice, it produces working code or configured software that proves a solution is feasible and exposes its constraints early.

Covers prototypes at every fidelity, from paper sketches and clickable mockups to coded prototypes built in the medium of the finished product.

Sanity

Sanity is a content management system whose content lives in a hosted, real-time datastore, the Content Lake, is queried with GROQ, and is edited in Sanity Studio, an open-source React application that teams configure in code with schema types, desk structure, custom inputs, document actions and plugins.

Applies to writing about working with Sanity itself: configuring or extending Sanity Studio, defining schemas, writing GROQ queries, building with Sanity's plugins, functions and APIs, and Sanity's own events and builder community.

Card Sorting

Card sorting is a user research method in which participants group cards labeled with content items or terms into categories that make sense to them, revealing how they expect information to be grouped and labeled.

Tree Testing

Tree testing is an evaluation method in which participants look for given items in a text-only hierarchy of labels, testing whether a proposed structure and its labels match where people expect to find information.

Domain Modeling

Domain modeling is a contextual research method that produces a structured representation of the key concepts in a subject area and the salient relationships between them, so that later structural design rests on how the domain itself is organized.

User Interface Design

User interface design is a design practice concerned with the visible, operable surface of a product: the layout, typography, color, controls and visual hierarchy through which people perceive content and act on it, and the way that surface adapts across screen sizes and devices.

Includes visual design, responsive layout and systems of reusable interface components.

Site Maps

A site map is an information architecture model of a website's structure: its pages or page types and the hierarchical and navigational relationships among them. Usually drawn as an organization-chart style diagram, it is used to plan, communicate and review a site's structure with a team.

Covers site maps as design artifacts, including their limits for large, changing content collections and the alternatives that model the same structure.

Content Operations

Content operations is a content strategy practice concerned with running content as an ongoing function: the people, workflows, tools and policies through which an organization produces, reviews, maintains and retires content at scale, and keeps the structures that support it current as needs change.

Includes governance: the decision rights, rules and maintenance routines that keep content, models and vocabularies effective over time.

Web Writing

Web writing is a content strategy practice concerned with the words themselves: writing and editing for how people read on screens, where they scan, search and arrive in the middle of a journey, with language that is clear, concise and consistent across a site.

Includes editorial style guides and the voice, tone and terminology guidance that keeps a team's writing consistent.

Discovery

Discovery is the design practice of learning what can be known about a product or content collection before and while changing it: what it holds, who uses it and why, the conditions it operates in, and what it costs and returns to build and maintain.

Structural Analysis

Structural analysis is both a content discovery and an evaluation method: the systematic assessment of how a content collection is built, including its content types, the attributes they are composed of and the relationships between elements in a given implementation, in order to keep what works and improve what does not.

Human Centered Design

Human-centered design is a design approach that grounds every decision in the needs, abilities, goals and contexts of the people who will use what is being designed. It involves those people throughout the work, through research and iterative evaluation, rather than starting from the technology or the organization's structure.

Includes user-centered design, and the human-centered design process codified in ISO 9241-210.

Goals

Goals are project management assets that capture the objectives a project exists to achieve, whether for the business, its users or the organization, together with the work of defining, prioritizing and agreeing on them. Agreed upon goals give scope, design decisions and measures of success something to be traced back to.

Includes success criteria and the measures used to tell whether a goal has been met.

Use Cases

Use cases is a project management assets that describe the specific situations in which people or systems will use what is being built, covering who is acting, what they are trying to accomplish and in what circumstances. Identifying and documenting them grounds requirements, scope and priorities in concrete needs rather than in features.

Includes user stories, scenarios and the requirements derived from them.

Natural Language Processing

Natural language processing is an engineering practice that uses computational methods to analyze, interpret or generate human language, turning unstructured text into data that software can work with. Typical tasks include extracting keywords and entities, classifying and clustering documents, and measuring how similar two texts are.

Includes statistical and machine learning techniques applied to text, from term frequency analysis to embeddings and semantic similarity. Concerns the techniques; the models and services that apply them are engineering tools.

Standards Compliance

Standards compliance is an engineering practice of building systems, content and data to conform to published, consensus-based specifications, such as those for markup, accessibility, metadata and vocabularies. Working to a shared standard lets the results behave predictably across browsers, platforms and organizations, and keeps them usable as tools change.

Includes adopting a standard deliberately as the basis for a design or implementation, as well as testing conformance to it.

Programming Languages

A programming language is an engineering tool used to write operational code: a formal notation, with its own syntax and rules, for expressing programs or queries that a computer can execute. Languages differ in what they are designed for, from general-purpose programming to querying a particular kind of data.

SPARQL

SPARQL is a query language, standardized by the W3C, for retrieving and updating data stored as RDF. Its queries match patterns of subject–relationship–object statements, so they can follow chains of relationships through a graph and combine data published at separate endpoints.

Engineering Products

An engineering product is an engineering tool delivered as a ready-made application, platform or service that a team adopts and configures rather than writes: the systems that store, manage, process and deliver content and data.

CMS

A content management system is a product for creating, storing, organizing and publishing content, pairing an editing interface for authors with a content repository and a means of delivering content to websites and other channels. A headless CMS separates the repository from presentation and delivers structured content through an API to any number of front ends.

Continuous Integration

Continuous integration is an engineering practice employed to automatically build, test and deploy software whenever changes are committed to a shared code repository, running defined workflows in a clean environment so that problems surface early and every release follows the same repeatable steps.

Includes continuous deployment, and workflows that rebuild and publish a site when its content changes.

AI

AI is a class of products that perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as generating and summarizing text, answering questions and classifying information, using models trained on large amounts of data. It is most often encountered as large language models offered through assistants, services and programming interfaces.

Covers AI models and the assistants and services built on them: what they are, how they behave, and their strengths and limits in practice.

Graph Databases

A graph database is a product that stores data as nodes and the relationships between them, rather than as rows in tables, so that connected data can be queried by following relationships directly. Its structure can grow incrementally, adding new kinds of things and relationships without reorganizing what is already stored.

Includes both triple stores and labeled property graph databases.

Frameworks

A framework is an engineering tool that supplies a reusable structure of conventions, components and rules within which something is built, so that work starts from an established foundation rather than from scratch. Software frameworks structure how applications and websites are built; data frameworks structure how information is described and exchanged.

RDF

RDF is a data framework, standardized by the W3C, for describing information as statements, each linking a subject to an object through a named relationship. Because things and relationships are identified by URIs, statements from different sources can be merged into a single graph and queried together.

Includes RDF serializations such as Turtle, and the languages layered on RDF for schemas, ontologies and validation, such as RDFS, OWL and SHACL.

Astro

Astro is a JavaScript framework for building content-driven websites. It renders pages to static HTML at build time by default, ships client-side JavaScript only for the components that need interactivity, and can draw content from a headless content management system or run as a server for pages rendered on request.

Design Outcomes

A design outcome is an outcome that shows up in how well a product serves its intended audience: a quality of a content collection or information space, achieved through decisions about structure, interactions, labeling and relationships, and judged by how readily its audiences can find, understand and use what it holds.

Interoperability

Interoperability is an engineering outcome that ensures content and data can be accessed and used by connected systems, services, and agents. Part of the FAIR data recommendation (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable).

Content Reuse

Content reuse is a design outcome in which content is created once and used in more than one place, channel or context, published as is or repurposed, rather than being rewritten or duplicated for each.

Discoverability

Discoverability is a design outcome in which content, and the concepts, facts and ideas it holds, can be found and understood by the audiences it is intended for. It depends on how content is organized, labeled and connected, and on how well that matches what those audiences already know and expect.

Engineering Outcomes

An engineering outcome is an outcome that shows up in systems and data themselves: a property of how content and data are encoded, stored and exchanged, achieved through implementation choices about formats, schemas and infrastructure, and judged by what software, services and agents can do with the result.

Machine Readability

Machine readability is an engineering outcome in which content and data are encoded so that software can interpret their meaning, not merely display them: entities, facts and relationships are explicitly typed and structured, so that search engines, voice assistants, AI agents and other systems can retrieve, combine and act on them without human interpretation.

Covers the quality and the case for pursuing it, in content and markup as well as in data.

Structured Content

Structured content is a design outcome in which organized, predictable, and consistent content that can be easily reused, repurposed, and understood by both humans and machines across various platforms and contexts. It is often marked up using specific languages to enhance usability and accessibility, and it is broken down into discrete, meaningful pieces for optimal management, interpretation, and display.
